notes.title: Lost Legions Kickstarter: Coming Soon!
notes.content:
🚀 Big news, everyone! We're gearing up to launch the Lost Legions Kickstarter campaign, and we need your support to make it happen!

We've recently gone live with our pre-launch page, and this is where we need your support. 
The more followers we get on the pre-launch, the faster we can officially launch the campaign. 

It’s as simple as hitting "Follow"! Think of it as joining the legion before the battle begins.


{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/d1d609a7b7435b17359973764ea2df85669d6f77.jpg

Why follow now?

By following, you’ll be the first to know when we officially launch, so you can grab those early-bird rewards!
You’ll help us build momentum, showing the world the strength of our community.

It’s a small action with a huge impact—pushing us one step closer to realizing this Roman Empire survival adventure.

How you can help:

- Follow the  pre-launch page   - it takes just a click! 
- Share it with your friends, family, or anyone who loves Roman history or survival games.

Thanks for standing with us - we can’t wait to show you more.

notes.title: Weekly Blog 18
notes.content:
Hi everyone!

Felix here with another episode of our weekly blog. I’m still reeling from Gamescom. Having my own booth for the first time felt completely unreal. For three days between 10am and 6pm we had visitors from potential publishers and from the press come in in 30min intervals to see the hands off demo we had prepared for Gamescom. Pitching the game so many times in front of so many people, answering their questions and seeing their reactions was a real boon. I have the feeling I know my own game so much better and have a much clearer vision now than I did before. The biggest takeaway came from talking to wonderful people from an experienced survival games publisher/developer that hammered in how important a good fighting system will be for a game based on ancient Rome. I’ll have more to say about that in a later blog.

For now I would like to present you with the following video I made shortly after gamescom. In this 26 min long video, you’ll see a full playthrough of the Gamescom demo, where we demonstrate many of the core mechanics and features we've been developing. I’ll walk you through our vision and how we've started implementing your feedback in this early version. In English.

[previewyoutube=oFJwM_SzYHg;full][/previewyoutube]

I recorded this video as an experiment. The experience at gamescom made us realize that you, our community, are the most important part of this journey and that we want to find better ways to interact with you and get your feedback. With this in mind our discord community got the first look a last week accompanied with the following questions:


 What gameplay elements or mechanics stood out to you the most in the demo? Why?
 Were there any moments or features that you found confusing or unclear? How do you think they could be improved?
 Which aspects of the game would you like to see expanded or developed further?
 What are your thoughts on the current art style and visuals? Do they match the tone and theme of the game?
 Did any particular visual elements or designs catch your eye? Why do you think they worked well?
 Do you think the long-form video would make for a good marketing beat? Should we make it public?


We received great feedback and I followed it up with an answer that I’m sharing with you here verbatim:

—
Thanks again for all the feedback you provided. It’s terrifying and so interesting at the same time to show our baby for the first time and read your thoughts. A bit like when you put your hands on your face in a horror movie and peek between the fingers to not miss any of the action.

In the end it was really helpful and gave me confidence that we are on the right path. The most
positive feedback was consistent with what we identify as USPs ourselves and the most negative ones mostly fit with what bothers us in the game as well. On top of that there were a lot of thought-provoking ideas in there that will definitely flow in future design discussions we have.

There's 2 ways I want to answer you as a whole:

[olist]
 Reflect what I took as the biggest points from the feedback to you and give you a chance to check me if I forgot something. I’ll occasionally add my thoughts directly in underlined text.
 Answer some questions and give insights to some of the thought processes behind our decisions. Feel free to give constructive criticism there as well.
[/olist]

Here are the biggest points and questions from the feedback, I used AI to help me categorize:

General Positive Feedback:

 Blueprint Building Mechanic: Highlighted for ease of use and thoughtful.
 Centralized Inventory (Global Inventory): Praised as a significant quality-of-life improvement, avoiding excessive running back and forth.
 Task Delegation/Worker Assignment: Smooth implementation appreciated, with potential concerns for future scaling or expansion.


This was all really cool to see as that is exactly what we wanted to shine a light on with the demo. (USPs)

General Concerns:

 NPC Behavior/Animations: Multiple respondents found NPC animations out of sync or unnatural. – This has been a pain since the very beginning. As a small team we need to develop a sturdy yet lightweight pipeline to be able to deliver facial expressions, in sync with voice over, in sync with body animations. From a technical POV these are separate channels that need to play nice with each other. We are getting there and made tremendous progress however what you see in the demo is a fast and rough treatment and basically a proof of concept. More to come.
 Combat Mechanics: A lack of dynamic combat stances, with requests for features like shield walls and troop formations. – This is something that has been making us very excited since we had the same feedback at Gamescom. Very high on the to-do if we get an investment. We might get to improve the 1v1 combat quite a bit without any investment thanks to better animations but formations (what really excites me) will not be feasible without more budget.
 Character Creation/Progression: Requests for more customization in multiplayer and clarity on character strengths/weaknesses. – Character customization is a bottomless pit in terms of production investment. We’re thinking of taking the path of games like Grounded where characters have predefined looks and personalities but are the same in terms of initial abilities.


General Questions:

 Players were unsure about the mechanics for accessing and using the command table to assign tasks. – This part of the controls and the UI is still very rough. The way I ordered NPCswas by pressing Q on objects that could be assigned tasks. We will improve on this for the next public version.
 Some respondents felt unclear about how the stockpile is organized and whether there is a limit on storage capacity. – The idea is that the stockpile is an endless storage. Potentially it will be restricted and you will be able to build boxes that will extend the capacity of the storage in general. This needs to be tested.
 There was a question about whether workers would stop tasks to defend the camp if an attack occurred while they were working. – The way they work now they would be slaughtered like sheep. ^^ The idea is that they switch to combat mode themselves and go defend the base and themselves.


2. Visuals & Art Style
Common Positive Feedback:

 Armor & Buildings: Roman-themed visuals were well received, with armor and environmental textures often standing out.
 Hostile Environment: The inclusion of worn-down NPCs with scratches and environmental elements like burning forests added to the atmosphere. - I’m sure our Lead Artist Tim will be happy to hear that. :)


Common Concerns:

 Art Style Uniqueness: While some players liked the gritty and realistic style, others suggested the need for a more unique or identifiable aesthetic to stand out. - I feel that might be a common problem with realistic games. I’d be happy to hear more concrete ideas on how to make it more unique if you have any.


Questions:

 Some players were confused about how players will be notified if resources are unavailable (e.g., wood for building) – Probably through a notification when the problem arises and through a visible issue marker in the management interface.

Suggestions for Improvement:

 Lighting & Ambiance: Some respondents mentioned weather effects, fog, and environmental animations (like tree sway) could add more depth and immersion.


3. Narrative/Storytelling
Common Positive Feedback:

 Setting & Lore: The Roman-Germanic historical setting was well received as unique and underexplored in games.
 Tone-Setting Scenes: One respondent suggested adding narrative cutscenes to set the tone of the story and help the player connect with the protagonist. – The concrete idea there was to do something similar as Guild Wars 2 but with vignettes instead of an actual cutscene. Medieval Dynasties and Enshrouded do this as well. - I love it. The key I feel here is to make it as long as it needs to be and as short as possible.


Common Concerns:

 Historical Accuracy: Some respondents noted issues with the historical accuracy of names and roles (e.g., women in command roles) within a Roman legion. – I hear you on the names thing. Definitely something we didn’t look at with our historical advisor while making the demo.


On the topic of women in the Roman Legion: We’ve heard this one a lot lately and we took some time to think about it. On the one hand of course, we want the game to be as historically accurate as possible and on the other we don’t want to exclude half of our players by being strict on this issue. The solution we came up with is the following: NPCs will follow historical findings (no female legionaries, but holding other roles and positions on both sides). The players on the other hand will be free to play whoever they want, including the most badass female Optio the world has never seen.

4. User Interface (UI)
Common Concerns:

 Crafting Indicators: Several respondents felt the UI for quick slots and crafting timers was too modest or overlapped with other text.
 NPC Assignment Clarity: Some confusion on how NPCs are activated to perform tasks. 


The UI is still very much work in progress. We’ll definitely put a focus on the points that stood out to you the most.

5. Marketing & Publicity
Common Consensus:

 Marketing Strategy: Respondents felt the current demo video was too long and not polished enough for public marketing. Shorter, more focused videos (e.g., clips on TikTok) were suggested.

                                                                                
I hear you. Thanks for the reality check. I’m sure Bat-El feels validated. ^^ We’ll make shorter, more specific videos about each topic. This long form video will be shown in a blog post on steam at some point to get the wider community up to speed with you.

Miscellaneous/Other Feedback

 More Pets & Dynamic NPC Behavior: Requests for more interactive NPCs (like cooks working). – We’re actively working on that. It’s a bit tricky because they will need to interact with dynamically placed objects.
 More animals to pet. – Yes! Always! More! My secret wish is to take the doggo in battle… but then he could get hurt… which I probably couldn’t stomach.
 Motion Sickness: Rapid camera movement caused discomfort for one player. – Super important Topic. I have no clue about that topic from a design standpoint but we’ll dive into this. We have our own motion sickness patient with Uschi that we can test our solutions on. *mad scientist laughter*

—

And that’s it! While we’ve already gotten a lot of quality feedback please don’t hesitate to reach out with more. Join our discord server if you haven’t already to get access to more sneak peeks of that nature before anybody else. Since we use discord to work we’re also more responsive there.

Puh. That was a long one. ^^ I’ll leave you here to get back to the pixel mines. That game is not going to make itself!

See you next time!
Felix

notes.title: Weekly Blog 8
notes.content:
Salvete amici mei,
In the best sense of a developer diary, today I'm sharing with you what has occupied us over the past week.

The biggest change in our mode is certainly the start of the internship period.

Back in early March, I introduced our studio and the project to the students for the first time at the S4G Recruitment Day. Since then, an application process took place, resulting in eight (8!) interns.

Last week, we finally moved into a room at the S4G School for Games as a co-working space, where the core team also has the opportunity to leave the confines of their home offices and return to staring at monitors and loading bars in real human company.

We’ve been working together for a week now, and I couldn’t be happier with our new circumstances. Everyone is super committed, fully immersed in the project both mentally and practically, and has high standards for themselves and our game.

Thanks to this support, we are able to tackle some topics that we otherwise wouldn’t have been able to address in the alpha phase.

Character & Environment Concept Art 
- We are using Unreal’s Metahumans. Despite all the advantages, it quickly becomes clear: the base characters are very generic. Thanks to the developed backstories for each character, our concept artist can create designs to make the characters look more interesting. 

- The most important character in Lost Legions is certainly the environment. To give the locations in the game the right atmosphere, another artist is designing distinctive interaction points and landmarks. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/eff5a2e115f766bd3be5954dc670e5e2ea779247.png

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/dcbc3faa69508214d253e0f9f0b266cc0ed7c9fb.png

UX Flow and UI Design 
To develop quickly and efficiently, our game is based on a combination of pre-made frameworks. We omit certain functions, expand others, or add new ones. To turn this mosaic back into a cohesive and easily understandable whole, the user interface must be well planned and designed. For this important task, we were able to secure a dedicated designer. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/20ce1a74f91d06ad0bfcdb8e69a14c649fd17edd.png

Level and Quest Design 
Under Uschi’s leadership, two other interns are working on the actual implementation of the game content. What is there to discover? What is my goal? Who stands in my way and what is the reward for my effort? In this exciting area, all fields of work come together. Scenography, lighting, camera, sound, and acting down to the fog machine, everything has to be considered.

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/51c6382705f571068f2a7de2ce818f85eaef07db.png

Combat Effects (Blood & Gore!!) 
An important aspect of the game that we want to improve by the alpha milestone in August is combat. A function we have lacked so far, but from which we hope for a big impact, is visual effects as feedback for player inputs. To put it simply: blood should splatter, sparks should fly. 
Players should clearly see whether they hit or get hit. An experienced programmer, who uses the S4G training program to specialize in this area, is creating something splashy for us. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/39e4b8d997a2d480bc1d1c177cf838a47276e901.gif

Behavior of Animals and NPCs 
Another trainee programmer is supporting Felix and Stephan from the core team to bring better NPC behaviors into the game. Our first project is to see if we can make Unreal’s standard wolf and deer more believable and, from a player’s perspective, give them more interesting behavior. 

Improvement of Animations 
Together with a talented 3D and tech artist, I am setting up a pipeline to improve or replace the currently used animations. We are looking for solutions to add more bones to the Metahuman skeleton to handle certain special cases. Right now, we are even experimenting with AI-supported solutions like Cascadeur. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/a0c8ac84025907edc875573d52f19cdcee946732.png

More Items, Clothing 
Incidentally, he is also creating more objects to fill in some content gaps, so that the demo at Gamescom appears as comprehensive as possible. For example, he implemented a clever system to apply fur, based on a modern programmatic solution using Blender’s Geometry Nodes. 

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/26fd69514c4e6f9b5b2214a2c2ce080b631fa2fc.gif

{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44992326/fa2b3f34a4ccf26120eded6b421a13b1cb7c70de.gif

As hoped and (to be honest) also planned, the handpicked students are doing excellent work. 
This is of course a testament to each and every one of them, who bring their creativity and work ethic to our service. But I also want to point out that the training at S4G School for Games proves to me every year that it trains directly for the industry. 
The graduates are so familiar with the usual workflows of the games industry that they can jump right in without lengthy onboarding. As a studio, we get additional manpower, which we are very grateful for right before Gamescom. The trainees get the opportunity to contribute to a commercial game development as part of their training and will be credited at the end. 

I am looking forward to the time together and the great new content in the game that we will create together.

Best regards, 

Jens
